title.en: Olorun, the Owner of the Idle Sky
title.zh: 奧洛倫——閒逸的天之主

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the vaulted sky over Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費上空的穹蒼）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Olorun is the deified firmament, the solid vaulted roof of the world, but he is too distant or too indifferent to interfere in human affairs: he dozes in idleness, keeps no priests, images or temples, and receives worship only in a few set phrases — thanks for the morning sun, and invocations at night that the roof of the world may hold.
summary.zh: 奧洛倫是被神化的蒼穹——覆護大地的固態拱頂。他太遠、太淡漠，不問人間事，終日打盹安眠；無祭司、無神像、無廟宇，人間只在晨間致謝與夜間祝禱的套語中略及於他，盼這世界的屋頂夜夜安在。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. Ellis's 1894 colonial ethnography describes a high sky-god of the dozing, uninvolved type; compare the myth-registered distinction between Olorun and the active orishas.

passages.text: Olorun is the sky-god of the Yorubas, that is, the deified firmament, or personal sky. The name means Owner of the Sky, and the sky is believed to be a solid body, curving over the earth so as to cover it with a vaulted roof. Like his counterparts on the Slave Coast, Olorun is considered too distant, or too indifferent, to interfere in the affairs of the world. The natives say that he enjoys a life of complete idleness and repose, a blissful condition according to their ideas, and passes his time dozing or sleeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Since he is too lazy or too indifferent to exercise any control over earthly affairs, man does not waste time in propitiating him, but reserves worship and sacrifice for more active agents; hence Olorun has no priests, symbols, images, or temples. His name occurs chiefly in set phrases: the proper reply to the morning salutation "Have you risen well?" is "Thanks to Olorun," and "May Olorun protect you" is sometimes heard in the evening, an invocation of the firmament, the roof of the world, to remain above and protect the earth during the night. A proverb fixes his limits: "A man cannot cause rain to fall, and Olorun cannot give you a child" — forming a child in the womb being the office of Obatala, for each god has his own duties and cannot trespass upon the rights of others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Odudua Blind: The Quarrel in the Closed Calabash
title.zh: 瞎眼的奧杜杜瓦——合葫蘆中的爭吵

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the closed calabash of Heaven and Earth)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：天地合葫蘆之形）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: In the beginning, the earth-goddess Odudua and her husband Obatala lay shut in a great closed calabash, in darkness, hungry and cramped. When her complaints turned to a violent quarrel, Obatala tore out her eyes; in return she cursed him, "Naught shalt thou eat but snails" — which is why snails are still offered to Obatala.
summary.zh: 太初之時，地母奧杜杜瓦與夫君奧巴塔拉同閉於一只大葫蘆中，黑暗無光，飢寒侷促。抱怨化為激烈爭吵，奧巴塔拉怒而挖出她的雙眼；她反咒：「你但食蝸牛，別無他物！」——這便是今日仍以蝸牛祭奧巴塔拉之由。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; cosmogonic quarrel of the divine couple recorded in 1894 colonial ethnography. Snail offerings to Obatala are part of ongoing devotion.

passages.text: According to a myth, Odudua is blind. In the beginning of the world she and her husband Obatala were shut up in darkness in a large, closed calabash, Obatala being in the upper part and Odudua in the lower. The myth does not state how they came to be in this situation, but they remained there for many days, cramped, hungry, and uncomfortable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Odudua began complaining, blaming her husband for the confinement; and a violent quarrel ensued, in the course of which, in a frenzy of rage, Obatala tore out her eyes, because she would not bridle her tongue. In return she cursed him, saying, "Naught shalt thou eat but snails," which is the reason why snails are now offered to Obatala. As the myth does not make Odudua recover her sight, she must be supposed to have remained sightless, but no native regards her as being blind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Odudua and the Hunter of Ado
title.zh: 奧杜杜瓦與阿多獵人

region.en: Ado, Nigeria (symbolic pin: silk-cotton tree north of Badagry)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿多城（象徵定位：巴達格利北的木棉樹下）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Odudua, patroness of love, met a handsome hunter alone in the forest, and the two lived for weeks in a hut of branches at the foot of a great silk-cotton tree. When her passion cooled she left him, but promised to protect all who settled at the spot; a town grew up and was named Ado in memory of its origin, with a temple where, on her feast days, women abandon themselves to male worshippers in her honour.
summary.zh: 愛之守護女神奧杜杜瓦在林中邂逅俊美獵人，二人於大木棉樹下的枝葉棚中同居數週。熱情冷卻後她離去，卻允諾庇佑所有在彼定居之人；聚落漸成，城名「阿多」以紀其緣起，並建神廟；節慶之日，婦女們以肉身敬奉女神。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; temple-cult origin legend of Ado with a licensed festival described in 1894 ethnographic terms. Content referenced without graphic detail.

passages.text: Odudua is patroness of love, and many stories are told of her adventures and amours. Her chief temple is in Ado, the principal town of the state of the same name. The word Ado means a lewd person of either sex, and its selection for the name of this town is accounted for by the following legend: Odudua was once walking alone in the forest when she met a hunter, who was so handsome that the ardent temperament of the goddess at once took fire. The advances which she made to him were favourably received, and they forthwith mutually gratified their passion on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: After this the goddess became still more enamoured, and, unable to tear herself away, lived with him for some weeks in a hut which they constructed of branches at the foot of a large silk-cotton tree. At the end of this time her passion had burnt out, and, having become weary of the hunter, she left him; but before doing so she promised to protect him and all others who might come and dwell in the favoured spot where she had passed so many pleasant hours. In consequence many people came and settled there, and a town gradually grew up, which was named Ado to commemorate the circumstances of its origin. A temple was built for the protecting goddess; and there, on her feast days, sacrifices of cattle and sheep are made, and women abandon themselves to the male worshippers in her honour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Yemaja Bursts Asunder, and the Gods Are Born at Ife
title.zh: 耶莫雅身裂眾神誕於伊費

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the spot where Yemaja's body burst open)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（耶莫雅身裂之地）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Yemaja, daughter of Heaven and Earth, wed her brother Aganju and bore Orungan, the Air — who ravished her. As she fled weeping and he seized at her, she fell, her body swelled frightfully, two streams gushed from her breasts to make a lagoon, and from her burst body came fifteen offsprings: Dada, Shango, Ogun, Olokun, Olosa, Oya, Oshun, Oba, Orisha Oko, Oshosi, Oke, Aje Shaluga, Shankpanna, the Sun and the Moon. On the spot the town of Ife was built — the holy city, whose name means distention, enlargement, swelling up.
summary.zh: 天與地之女耶莫雅嫁兄阿甘朱，生下「天際高處」奧倫岡——天空與大地之間的氣。他竟淫侵母親；耶莫雅奔逃哀泣，被追及撲倒，肚腹膨脹可怖，雙乳噴出兩道水柱匯成潟湖，裂開的軀體中誕下十五位神祇：達達、尚戈、奧貢、奧洛貢、奧洛薩、奧雅、奧舜、奧巴、農神奧科、獵神奧索西、山神奧凱、財神阿傑、痘神香潘納，以及日與月。裂身之處建城名「伊費」——意為鼓脹、漲大——遂為約魯巴聖城。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; central theogony of the Yemaja cycle (Ellis 1894). Includes a rape episode, reported as the recorded myth states it. Ife remains a living sacred city.

passages.text: Before her amour with the hunter, Odudua bore to her husband Obatala a boy and a girl, named respectively Aganju and Yemaja: the offspring of the union of Heaven and Earth, representing Land and Water. Yemaja is the goddess of brooks and streams and presides over ordeals by water. Yemaja married her brother Aganju, and bore a son named Orungan — "In the height of the sky" — who seems to answer to the free-air region between sky and earth: the offspring of Land and Water would thus be what we call Air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Orungan fell in love with his mother, and as she refused to listen to his guilty passion, he one day took advantage of his father's absence and ravished her. Immediately after the act Yemaja sprang to her feet and fled from the place wringing her hands and lamenting, pursued by Orungan, who strove to console her, holding out the alluring prospect of living with two husbands, one acknowledged and the other in secret; but she rejected all his proposals with loathing and continued to run away. He rapidly gained upon her and was just stretching out his hand to seize her when she fell backward to the ground. Then her body immediately began to swell in a fearful manner, two streams of water gushed from her breasts, and her abdomen burst open. The streams joined and formed a lagoon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: From her gaping body came the following: Dada, god of vegetables; Shango, god of lightning; Ogun, god of iron and war; Olokun, god of the sea; Olosa, goddess of the lagoon; Oya, goddess of the river Niger; Oshun, goddess of the river Oshun; Oba, goddess of the river Oba; Orisha Oko, god of agriculture; Oshosi, god of hunters; Oke, god of mountains; Aje Shaluga, god of wealth; Shankpanna, god of small-pox; Orun, the sun; and Oshu, the moon. To commemorate this event a town, given the name of Ife — distention, enlargement, swelling up — was built on the spot where Yemaja's body burst open, and became the holy city of the Yoruba-speaking tribes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango's Brazen Palace and His Fiery Stones
title.zh: 尚戈的銅宮與火石

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the storm clouds over Oyo)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：奧約上空雷雲）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Shango the thunder-god dwells in the clouds in an immense brazen palace with a great retinue and many horses, for he is also god of the chase and of pillage. Stone implements long out of use are his thunderbolts, hurled against those who offend him; when a house is struck, his priests rush in to plunder it and find the stone, while the worshippers cry through the streets that Shango is the lord and master who hurls his fiery stones against his enemies.
summary.zh: 雷神尚戈居於雲中廣袤的銅宮，僕從如雲、駿馬成群——他亦是狩獵與劫掠之神。古已不用的石器即其雷石，凡得罪於他者，他便自銅宮擲下。房屋遭雷擊，祭司即入內掠奪並尋出「雷石」；信眾於暴雨中沿街高呼：尚戈乃大王，於黑暗中擲火石擊敵，其光軌燁然。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Shango devotion remains active across Yorubaland and the Americas (as Shango/Chango in Santeria). Recorded 1894; presented as archival record.

passages.text: Shango, the god of thunder and lightning, is, next to Obatala, the most powerful god of the Yorubas; he was the second to spring from the body of Yemaja. He has the epithet of Jakuta, "Hurler of stones," or "Fighter with stones"; and stone implements, which have long ceased to be used in West Africa, are believed to be his thunderbolts. Shango is purely anthropomorphic. He dwells in the clouds in an immense brazen palace, where he maintains a large retinue and keeps a great number of horses; for, besides being the thunder-god, he is also the god of the chase and of pillage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: From his palace Shango hurls upon those who have offended him red-hot stones (or, in a newer notion, chains forged for him by his brother Ogun). A chant of his priests very commonly heard runs: "Oh, Shango, thou art the master. Thou takest in thy hand thy fiery stones, to punish the guilty and satisfy thine anger. Everything that they strike is destroyed. Their fire eats up the forest, the trees are broken down, and all living creatures are slain." Whenever a house is struck by lightning his priests rush in a body to pillage it and find the stone, which they take away secretly. And during a thunderstorm his lay-worshippers flock into the streets crying: "Shango, Shango, Great King! In the storm he hurls his fiery stones against his enemies, and their track gleams in the midst of the darkness."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The King Who Would Not Die: Shango Descends at Kuso
title.zh: 王未嘗死——尚戈沉於庫索

region.en: Kuso (near Oyo-Ile), Nigeria (the pit where Shango descended into the earth)
region.zh: 奈及利亞庫索（近舊奧約，尚戈沉地之坑）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: The tyrant king of Oyo is sent parrots' eggs — the royal command to go to sleep — but flees instead, deserted by all but one wife and a slave, and hangs himself from an ayan tree. When the chiefs come, no corpse hangs there: only a deep pit with an iron chain, and Shango's voice talking beneath the earth. A temple rises over the pit, scoffers are burned by his fiery stones, and Kuso becomes a town; Shango is now King of Kuso, an orisha among the dead.
summary.zh: 奧約暴君收到一葫蘆鸚鵡蛋——即「國王該去長眠」的通牒——他不肯受縊，連夜出逃，眾叛親離，只剩一妻一奴，終在阿揚樹上自縊。諸老趕來尋屍，樹上空空，唯地上一深坑，鐵鏈一端外露，坑底隱聞尚戈與亡者交談。眾人於坑上立廟；嘲弄者遭火石焚城；庫索自此成鎮。「尚戈未死，已登神位，居於冥土眾生之中。」

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the historical-mythic deification of a King of Oyo, central to Shango cult. Contains suicide of the king as the recorded myth states it. Cross-tradition: deified king who descends alive (cf. sacred-kingship cluster).

passages.text: On to the older ideas of the thunder-god are now rapidly becoming grafted some later myths, which make Shango an earthly king who afterwards became a god. This Shango was King of Oyo, capital of Yoruba, and became so unbearable through rapacity, cruelty, and tyranny, that the chiefs and people at last sent him a calabash of parrots' eggs, in accordance with the custom already mentioned, with a message that he must be fatigued with the cares of government and that it was time for him to go to sleep. On receiving this intimation, Shango, instead of allowing himself to be quietly strangled by his wives, defied public opinion and endeavoured to assemble his adherents; and, when this failed, sought safety in flight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: He left the palace by night, intending to reach Tapa, beyond the Niger, his mother's native place, accompanied only by one wife and one slave, the rest of his household having deserted him. During the night the wife repented of her hasty action and also left him; so, when in the morning Shango found himself lost in the midst of a pathless forest, he had no one with him but his slave. They wandered without food for some days, seeking in vain for a path out of the forest, and at last Shango left his slave, saying, "Wait here till I return, and we will then try further." After waiting a long time the slave went in search of him, and before long found his corpse hanging by the neck from an ayan tree. Eventually the slave made his way to Oyo and told the news.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the chiefs and elders heard that Shango had hanged himself they were much alarmed, fearing to be held responsible for his death. They went with the priests to the place, but were unable to find the body, for it was no longer on the tree. They searched in every direction, and at last found a deep pit in the earth from which the end of an iron chain protruded. They stooped over the pit and listened, and could hear Shango talking down in the earth. They at once erected a small temple over the pit, and, leaving priests there to propitiate the new god, returned to Oyo and proclaimed: "Shango is not dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: He has become an orisha. He has descended into the earth and lives among the dead people, with whom we have heard him conversing." Some foolish townsfolk laughed and shouted, "Shango is dead. Shango hanged himself" — and in consequence Shango came in person with a terrific thunderstorm, killed many of the scoffers with his fiery stones, and set the town on fire, until the populace beat the scoffers to death and his anger was appeased. The place where Shango descended was called Kuso, and soon became a town, for many people went to dwell there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango Breathes Fire: The Charm He Shared with Oya
title.zh: 尚戈口噴烈焰——與奧雅分食的符藥

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the earth that opened beneath the thunderer)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：雷神腳下裂開的大地）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Another myth makes Shango an earthly king who obtained from his father Obatala a charm that, when eaten, let him vanquish all who opposed him. He ate most of it and left the rest with Oya, who promptly ate it herself; next morning both burst into flames when they spoke, terror emptied the palace, and Shango — knowing himself inferior to none — stamped the earth open and descended into it with his three wives, the iron chain left protruding.
summary.zh: 另一說：尚戈為人王時，其父奧巴塔拉授他以符藥，食之可克一切敵。他食其大部，餘者交奧雅保管，奧雅旋即偷食殆盡。翌日朝會，尚戈一開口便口吐烈焰，滿朝奔逃；奧雅訓斥宮女亦噴火，宮中為之一空。尚戈自覺神威無雙，遂偕三妻踏地而地裂，攜鐵鏈沉入地中，鏈端仍露於土外。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; variant of the Shango deification myth showing Mohammedan and classical (fire-breathing, earth-opening) influence noted by Ellis. Cross-ref: yoruba-shango-hanged-kuso.

passages.text: Another myth makes Shango the son of Obatala, and married to the three river goddesses Oya, Oshun, and Oba, but reigning as an earthly king at Oyo. One day Shango obtained from his father Obatala a powerful charm, which, when eaten, would enable him to vanquish all who opposed him. Shango ate most of the medicament, and then gave the rest to Oya to keep for him; but she, as soon as his back was turned, ate the rest herself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the chiefs and elders assembled at the palace as usual to judge the affairs of the people, and each spoke in his turn; but when it came to Shango's turn to speak, flames burst forth from his mouth, and all fled in terror. Oya, too, when she began to scold her women in the palace, similarly belched forth flames, so that everybody ran away and the palace was deserted. Shango now saw that he was, as a god, inferior to none; so calling his three wives to him, and taking in his hand a long iron chain, he stamped on the earth till it opened under him, and descended into it with his wives. The earth closed again over them, but the end of the chain was left protruding from the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango Wrestling Huisi on the Lagoon Shore
title.zh: 尚戈與胡伊西潟湖畔角力

region.en: Lokoro, near Porto Novo, Nigeria (the fight-site with its temples)
region.zh: 奈及利亞洛科羅（近波多諾伏，角力之地，立廟處）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Down in the earth Shango quarrelled with Oya over his stolen medicines, and she fled to the sea-god Olokun. The thunderer followed the Sun's track across the sky — hiding whenever the Sun looked round — to Olokun's palace, where he nearly seized her before Oya escaped to her sister Olosa. A man named Huisi, made an orisha by eating of her stolen medicines, tore up a tree to defy Shango; canoe and tree-shaft shattered together, and flames burst from their mouths as they wrestled — until Shango stamped the earth open and dragged Huisi down with him. Oya settled at Lokoro; both combatants got temples.
summary.zh: 尚戈在地中與奧雅為「藥」反目，奧雅懼而投奔海神兄長奧洛貢。尚戈尾隨太陽橫越天穹——太陽一回頭他便躲——直抵海底宮殿。奧雅逃往姊妹奧洛薩處；凡人胡伊西食其偷來之藥而成神，連根拔樹向雷神叫陣。舟與樹幹互撞而碎，二人角力、口噴烈焰、足裂大地，僵持不下——末了尚戈踏地而下，拖著胡伊西同沉。奧雅定居洛科羅，立廟；胡伊西亦有其廟。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; episode of the Shango–Oya cycle recorded by Ellis 1894. Huisi is a local deified hero near Porto Novo.

passages.text: Since his descent into the earth with his three wives at Oyo, Shango has often come back to the world. One day, when down in the earth, he quarrelled with Oya, who had stolen some of his medicines; and she, terrified at his violence, ran away and took refuge with her brother the Sea-God, Olokun. As soon as Shango discovered where she had gone, he swore a great oath to beat her so that she would never forget it. Next morning he came up from below with the Sun and, following him in his course all day, arrived with him in the evening at the place where the sea and sky join, and so descended with him into the territories of his brother Olokun — for the Sun had not knowingly shown Shango the road, the thunderer having kept behind him all the time, hiding when the Sun looked round.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Shango reached Olokun's palace and saw his wife Oya there, he made a great noise and commotion, and rushed towards her to seize her; but Olokun held him, and while the two were struggling together Oya escaped and ran to hide with her sister Olosa, the Lagoon. Released, Shango ran after his wife cursing and threatening, tearing up the trees by their roots as he ran and tossing them here and there. Looking out from her sister's house, Oya saw him coming along the banks of the lagoon; knowing that Olosa could not protect her, she ran out and fled along the shores towards the place where the Sun goes down. Near at hand she saw a house, rushed into it, and claimed protection of a man named Huisi. He asked what he, a man, could do against Shango; but Oya gave him to eat of the medicines she had stolen, and he, being thus made an orisha, promised to protect her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Shango approached, Huisi ran from his house down to the banks of the lagoon, and tearing up a large tree by the roots, brandished it in the air and defied Shango. There being no other tree there, Shango seized Huisi's canoe, shook it like a club, and the two weapons, striking together, were shattered to pieces. Then the two orishas wrestled together: flames burst from their mouths, and their feet tore great fissures in the earth as they dragged each other to and fro. The struggle lasted a long time without either gaining the mastery, and at last Shango, filled with fury at being baffled and feeling his strength failing, stamped on the earth, which opened under him, and he descended into it, dragging Huisi down with him. At the commencement of the combat Oya had fled to Lokoro; she remained there, and the people built a temple in her honour. Huisi, who had become a god by virtue of the medicine he had eaten, also had a temple erected to him on the spot where he had fought with Shango.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Ifa Plants the Palm-Nut at Ado
title.zh: 伊法在阿多種下棕櫚仁

region.en: Ado, Nigeria (the rock from which sixteen palm-trees grew)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿多城（十六棵棕櫚同生的巨石）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: Ifa, god of divination and of palm-nuts, first appeared on earth at Ife but was not listened to; he wandered the world teaching mankind, indulging in many amours, and fixed his residence at Ado, where he planted on a rock a single palm-nut from which sixteen palm-trees grew up at once.
summary.zh: 占卜之神、棕櫚之主伊法初現於伊費，無人肯聽其教；遂周遊世界教導凡人，情事繁多，最後定居阿多——在巨石上種下一粒棕櫚仁，頃刻之間，十六棵棕櫚一齊長成。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Ifa divination is UNESCO-listed intangible heritage (2008). Ellis 1894 colonial-era record presented as such.

passages.text: Ifa, god of divination, who is usually termed the God of Palm Nuts, because sixteen palm-nuts are used in the process of divination, comes after Shango in order of eminence. Ifa's secondary attribute is to cause fecundity: he presides at births, and women pray to him to be made fruitful, offerings being always made to him before marriage, it being considered a disgrace not to bear children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ifa first appeared on the earth at Ife, but he did not come from the body of Yemaja, and his parentage and origin are unexplained. He tried to teach the inhabitants of Ife how to foretell future events, but they would not listen to him, so he left the town and wandered about the world teaching mankind. After roaming about for a long time, and indulging in a variety of amours, Ifa fixed his residence at Ado, where he planted on a rock a palm-nut, from which sixteen palm-trees grew up at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: How Hungry Ifa Bought Divination from Elegba
title.zh: 飢神伊法向艾萊格巴買下占卜術

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: Orungan's palm plantation near Ado)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：阿多附近奧倫岡的棕櫚園）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. II

summary.en: In the early days, few people offered few sacrifices, and the hungry gods took to trades; Ifa fished without luck. The crafty Elegba promised to teach him to forecast the future if he won the sixteen palm-nuts from Orungan's two lofty palms — and stipulated the first choice of all offerings for ever. Orungan's monkeys dropped the kernels from the trees, his wife carried them on her back like a child, and Ifa learned the art, passing it to Orungan, the first babalawo; to this day the client's wife carries the nuts, and the priest salutes the couple's memory.
summary.zh: 太初人稀祭薄，眾神飢而各營生計；伊法捕魚不利。狡黠的艾萊格巴許諾授他預知之術，但要先取得奧倫岡園中兩株高棕櫚上的十六枚果仁——且索「凡有祭品，先挑一份」為永約。奧倫岡夫婦驅猴上樓，猴食紅肉擲下硬仁；其妻如抱孩兒般將果仁負於背。艾萊格巴如約授術，伊法轉授奧倫岡——第一位巴巴拉奧。至今問卜者之妻仍負果仁而行，祭司必先念誦夫婦之名以致敬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; etiological myth for the babalawo's ritual remembered in living Ifa practice (UNESCO-listed). Ellis 1894 record.

passages.text: The general belief is that Ifa possessed the faculty of divination from the beginning, but there is a myth which makes him acquire the art from the phallic god Elegba. In the early days of the world there were but few people on the earth, and the gods found themselves stinted in the matter of sacrifices to such an extent that, not obtaining enough to eat from the offerings made by their followers, they were obliged to have recourse to various pursuits in order to obtain food. Ifa, who was in the same straits as the other gods, took to fishing, with but small success; and one day, when he had failed to catch any fish at all and was very hungry, he consulted the crafty Elegba, who was also in want, as to what they could do to improve their condition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Elegba replied that if he could obtain the sixteen palm-nuts from the two palms that Orungan, the chief man, had in his plantation, he would show Ifa how to forecast the future, so that Ifa could use his knowledge in the service of mankind and receive an abundance of offerings — stipulating that in return for instructing Ifa in the art of divination, he should always be allowed the first choice of all offerings made. Ifa agreed, and going to Orungan asked for the sixteen palm-nuts. Orungan, eager to know what the future had in store for him, at once promised them; but the trees were too lofty to reach and their stems too smooth to climb, so he and his wife Orisha-bi drove some monkeys into the palms. No sooner were the monkeys up than they seized the nuts and, after eating the red pulp, threw the hard kernels down, where the couple picked them up; and Orisha-bi tied them in a bundle on her back as if she were carrying a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they carried the palm-nuts to Ifa. Elegba kept his promise and taught Ifa the art of divination, and Ifa in his turn taught Orungan, who thus became the first babalawo. It is in memory of these events that when a man wishes to consult Ifa, he takes his wife with him, if he be married, and his mother if he be single, who carries the sixteen palm-nuts tied up in a bundle on her back, like a child; and the babalawo, before consulting the god, always says, "Orungan, ajuba oh! Orisha-bi, ajuba oh!" — Orungan, I hold you in grateful remembrance; Orisha-bi, I hold you in grateful remembrance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. II (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Olokun's Flood, and the Seven Iron Chains
title.zh: 奧洛貢洪災與七條鐵鏈

region.en: Lagos coast, Nigeria (the low-lying shore Olokun overflows)
region.zh: 奈及利亞拉哥斯海岸（奧洛貢漫溢之低岸）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: A myth says that Olokun, enraged at mankind's neglect, tried to destroy them by overflowing the land and had drowned large numbers when Obatala interfered to save the remainder, forcing Olokun back to his palace and binding him with seven iron chains until he promised to abandon his design — perhaps, says Ellis, the memory of some ancient encroachment of the sea on the low sandy shores, still liable to be submerged at spring-tides.
summary.zh: 神話云：奧洛貢因世人怠慢而怒，欲漫陸滅人；大水已吞滅眾多生靈，奧巴塔拉出手救下餘者，逼退海神，以七條鐵鏈縛之於其海底宮殿，直至他立誓罷手。艾利斯推想，此說或源於海洋自古對低平沙岸的侵蝕——至今大潮仍可沒頂。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Yoruba flood myth (Olokun's deluge bound by Obatala), key to the cross-tradition flood cluster. Variant of same deluge told of Ifa's ascent (Ellis ch. II). Cross-refs: hebrew-noah-flood, norse-bergelmir-flood, manu-flood.

passages.text: Olokun, "he who owns the sea," is the sea-god of the Yorubas, one of those who came from the body of Yemaja. When Olokun is angry he causes the sea to be rough and stirs up a raging surf upon the shore; and it is he who drowns men, upsets boats or canoes, and causes shipwrecks. He is of human shape and black in colour, with long flowing hair, and resides in a vast palace under the sea, where he is served by sea-spirits, some human in shape, others partaking of the nature of fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: A myth says that Olokun, becoming enraged with mankind on account of their neglect of him, endeavoured to destroy them by overflowing the land; and had drowned large numbers when Obatala interfered to save the remainder, and forced Olokun back to his palace, where he bound him with seven iron chains till he promised to abandon his design. This, perhaps, has reference to some former encroachment of the sea upon the low-lying sandy shores, which are even now liable to be submerged at spring-tides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Elusu, the Scaly Wife on the Lagos Bar
title.zh: 拉哥斯沙洲上的鱗身妻——埃魯蘇

region.en: Lagos harbour bar, Nigeria (Elusu's home in the shifting sand)
region.zh: 奈及利亞拉哥斯港口沙洲（埃魯蘇之居所）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Olokun's wife Elusu lives in the harbour bar at Lagos: white, human in shape, but covered with fish-scales from below the breasts to the hips. The fish of the bar are sacred to her; anyone who catches them is repaid by capsized canoes and drowned crews, and a fisherman rash enough to work the bar would risk being thrown overboard by the other canoemen themselves.
summary.zh: 海神奧洛貢之妻埃魯蘇棲身拉哥斯港口沙洲：膚白如人，乳房以下至臀卻覆滿魚鱗。沙洲之魚皆為聖物，捕之者必遭翻舟滅頂之報；膽敢在沙洲下鉤的漁夫，恐怕不等神罰，先被同行拋入海中。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; local sea-goddess cult at the Lagos bar recorded 1894.

passages.text: Olokun has a wife named Olokun-su, or Elusu, who lives in the harbour bar at Lagos. She is white in colour and human in shape, but is covered with fish-scales from below the breasts to the hips. The fish in the waters of the bar are sacred to her, and should anyone catch them, she takes vengeance by upsetting canoes and drowning the occupants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man who should be so ill-advised as to attempt to fish on the bar would run a great risk of being thrown overboard by the other canoemen. Olokun-su is an example of a local sea-goddess, originally considered quite independent, being attached to the general god of the sea, and accounted for as belonging to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lame Small-Pox God Laughed Out of the Dance
title.zh: 被逐出舞會的跛足痘神

region.en: Yoruba bush (symbolic pin: Shankpanna's temple in the uninhabited bush)
region.zh: 約魯巴荒野（象徵定位：痘神荒野廟址）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Shankpanna, the small-pox god, is old and lame. At a merrymaking in Obatala's palace he tried to join the dance, stumbled and fell on his withered leg — and all the gods burst out laughing. In revenge he strove to infect them with small-pox until Obatala drove him off with his spear; thenceforth he was forbidden the company of the gods, an outcast dwelling in desolate tracts, whose temples are always built in the bush, apart from towns, and whose notice is drawn by whistling at night.
summary.zh: 痘神香潘納年老腿跛。眾神在奧巴塔拉宮中歌舞作樂，他也想加入共舞，卻因殘腿絆倒在地——滿座神祇哄堂大笑。他憤而欲散布天花以報復，被奧巴塔拉持矛驅逐。自此他被禁與眾神往來，淪為棄神，獨居荒僻之地；其廟必建於離村野外之叢林，夜間在其居所附近吹口哨，即會招致天花。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Shankpanna/Shakpana (Nana Buruku-related) smallpox cult recorded 1894. Epidemic-deity narratives are treated with care; presented as archival record.

passages.text: Shankpanna, or Shakpana, who also came from the body of Yemaja, is the Small-pox god, his name having reference to the pustules with which a small-pox patient is covered and to his character as a man-killer. He is accompanied by an assistant named Buku, who kills those attacked by small-pox by wringing their necks. Shankpanna is old and lame, and is depicted limping along with the aid of a stick; according to a myth he has a withered leg.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when the gods were all assembled at the palace of Obatala and were dancing and making merry, Shankpanna endeavoured to join in the dance, but, owing to his deformity, stumbled and fell. All the gods and goddesses thereupon burst out laughing, and Shankpanna, in revenge, strove to infect them with small-pox; but Obatala came to the rescue, and, seizing his spear, drove Shankpanna away. From that day Shankpanna was forbidden to associate with the other gods, and he became an outcast who has since lived in desolate and uninhabited tracts of country. Temples dedicated to him are always built in the bush, at some little distance from a town or village, with a view to keeping him away from habitations; and to whistle by night near one of his haunts is believed to be a certain way of attracting his notice and contracting the disease.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Shigidi, the Nightmare That Squats on the Breast
title.zh: 希吉迪——壓胸的夢魘

region.en: Yoruba sleeping-rooms (symbolic pin: night-time compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴臥室（象徵定位：伊費近郊夜半院落）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Shigidi is deified nightmare, a short, bulky clay-cone god through whom men gratify their hate in secret. Sacrificed to, he rides the night wind to the marked victim, squats on his breast and presses out his breath — unless the sleeper's tutelary god wakes him in time, whereupon Shigidi leaps off, falls on the earthen floor and vanishes, for he has power over man only during sleep.
summary.zh: 希吉迪是夢魘之神，形如矮胖的泥錐頭。懷恨者以祭品雇他行兇：他乘夜風直達仇家，蹲踞仇人胸口「壓出呼吸」；若仇人的守護神及時喚醒睡者，他一躍而下、觸地即隱——他只在人熟睡時才有權柄。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; nightmare-demon belief (compare Bahamas "hag" among Yoruba descent), recorded 1894.

passages.text: Shigidi, or Shugudu, is deified nightmare. The name appears to mean something short and bulky, and the god, or demon, is represented by a short, broad head made of clay, or by a thick, blunted cone of clay ornamented with cowries. Shigidi is an evil god, and enables man to gratify his hate in secret and without risk to himself. When a man wishes to revenge himself upon another he offers a sacrifice to Shigidi, who thereupon proceeds at night to the house of the person indicated and kills him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: His mode of procedure is to squat upon the breast of his victim and press out his breath; but it often happens that the tutelary deity of the sufferer comes to the rescue and wakes him, upon which Shigidi leaps off, falls upon the earthen floor, and disappears, for he only has power over man during sleep. The person who employs Shigidi and sends him out to kill must remain awake till the god returns, for if he were to fall asleep Shigidi would at that moment turn back and the mission would fail. Shigidi either travels on the wind or raises a wind to waft him along; the first symptom of his attack is a feeling of heat and oppression at the pit of the stomach, and a man who feels it falling asleep must rise at once and seek the protection of the god he usually serves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Aroni, the One-Legged Master of Forest Herbs
title.zh: 阿羅尼——獨腿林中藥師

region.en: Yoruba forest fastness (symbolic pin: deep forest near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴深林（象徵定位：伊費近郊密林深處）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Aroni, the forest-god, has one leg, a dog's head and a dog's tail, and knows all medicine. Those who meet him and run are devoured; those who stand their ground are led two or three months into the depths of the forest and taught the secrets of the plants — then dismissed with a single hair from his tail as proof of initiation. A whirlwind swirling the dead leaves is his manifestation.
summary.zh: 森林之神阿羅尼一目一腿，狗首犬尾，通曉百藥。林中遇他而逃跑者，必被吞噬；昂然而立、面無懼色者，則被引至林中秘所兩三個月，學盡草木藥性，臨別得他尾上一毛以為憑證。林間捲起枯葉的旋風，正是他現身之兆。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; herbalist-initiation figure recorded 1894. Presented as archival record.

passages.text: Aroni is the Forest-god, and, like Osanhin, the god of medicine, has a knowledge of medicine, though the cure of disease is not his special function. The name means One having a withered limb, and Aroni is always represented as of human shape but with only one leg, the head of a dog, and a dog's tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Aroni seizes and devours those who meet him in the forest and attempt to run away when they see him; but if a man faces him boldly and shows no sign of fear, he leads him to his dwelling in the fastnesses of the forest, and keeps him there for two or three months, during which time he teaches him the secrets of the plants and their medicinal properties. When the pupil has no more to learn Aroni dismisses him, giving him a hair from his tail to prove to the incredulous that he has really been initiated. An eddy of wind, rushing through the forest and swirling up the dead leaves, is considered a manifestation of Aroni.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Aja, the Foot-High Teacher of Herbs
title.zh: 阿賈——一尺高的采藥之師

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: vine thicket near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊藤叢）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Aja, a deity like Aroni but smaller than a child of two feet, carries off those who meet her into the depths of the forest and teaches them the medicinal properties of plants — but she never harms anyone. The aja vine that shares her name is used by women to cure inflamed breasts.
summary.zh: 阿賈是一位類似阿羅尼的神祇，身高不過一二尺。遇見她的人會被帶入森林深處，學習草木的藥性——但她從不傷人。與她同名的阿賈藤，至今仍為婦女醫治乳腺腫痛之藥。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; gentle forest-teacher deity recorded 1894.

passages.text: Aja, whose name appears to mean a wild vine, is a deity somewhat similar to Aroni. Like Aroni, she carries off persons who meet her into the depths of the forest, and teaches them the medicinal properties of plants; but she never harms anyone. Aja is of human shape, but very diminutive, she being only from one to two feet high. The aja vine is used by women to cure inflamed breasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oye, the Giant of the Harmattan
title.zh: 奧耶——哈馬丹風的巨人

region.en: North of Ilorin, Nigeria (the cavern whence the dry wind blows)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊洛林以北（乾風所出的巨洞）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Oye, the god of the Harmattan wind, is a giant who, according to some, lives in a cavern to the north of Ilorin, while others say he resides on the mountain named Igbeti, where Elegba is supposed to have his palace.
summary.zh: 哈馬丹風之神奧耶是位巨人。一說他住在伊洛林以北的巨洞中，另一說他棲於伊格貝蒂山——那裡也是艾萊格巴傳說中的宮殿所在。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; wind-deity fragment recorded 1894.

passages.text: Oye, the god of the Harmattan wind, is a giant who, according to some, lives in a cavern to the north of Ilorin, while others say that he resides on the mountain named Igbeti, where Elegba is supposed to have his palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Ibeji: Keeping the Lost Twin Among the Living
title.zh: 伊貝吉——讓逝去的雙生留在人間

region.en: Erapo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: twin shrine on the Lagos-Badagry lagoon)
region.zh: 奈及利亞埃拉波（象徵定位：拉哥斯至巴達格利間潟湖的雙生神廟）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Ibeji, the tutelary deity of twins, has for sacred animal a small black mangrove monkey that twins and their parents may not eat. When one of twins dies, the mother carries a small wooden figure of the dead child beside the surviving one — to keep the living child from pining and to give the departed spirit a dwelling that will not disturb its twin. At Erapo stands a celebrated temple of Ibeji, whither twins and their parents make pilgrimage from far around.
summary.zh: 伊貝吉是雙生子之守護神，聖獸為紅樹林中的小黑猴，雙生子及其父母不得食其肉。孿生之一夭折時，母親便雕一具小木偶隨存活的孩子隨身攜帶——既免活著的孩子思念成疾，也給亡靈一個居所，免擾同胞。埃拉波的伊貝吉大廟遠近聞名，雙生子與其父母千里朝聖。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Ibeji twin-cult (ere-ibeji figures) is a world-renowned living practice. The Yoruba Ibeji is the key African parallel in the twins motif cluster (cf. maya-popol-vuh-creation-twins, Romulus and Remus). Cross-refs: maya-popol-vuh-creation-twins.

passages.text: Ibeji, Twins, is the tutelary deity of twins. A small black monkey, generally found amongst mangrove trees, is sacred to Ibeji; offerings of fruit are made to it, and its flesh may not be eaten by twins or the parents of twins. This monkey is called Edon dudu, or Edun, and one of twin children is generally named after it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When one of twins dies, the mother carries, with the surviving child, a small wooden figure seven or eight inches long, roughly fashioned in human shape and of the sex of the dead child, to keep it from pining for its lost comrade and also to give the spirit of the deceased child something to enter without disturbing the living child. Such figures are nude, as an infant would be, with beads round the waist. At Erapo, a village on the lagoon between Lagos and Badagry, there is a celebrated temple to Ibeji, to which all twins, and the parents of twins, from a long distance round make pilgrimages.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oshumare, the Rainbow-Serpent of the Underneath
title.zh: 奧舒馬雷——地底彩虹巨蛇

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: rainbow arching above the earth's rim, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費附近天際虹弧）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Oshumare is the Rainbow-god, the Great Snake of the Underneath, who comes up at times above the edge of the earth to drink water from the sky; the python called ere is his sacred messenger. By some accounts he serves Shango, carrying water from the earth up to the thunderer's palace in the clouds.
summary.zh: 彩虹之神奧舒馬雷是「地底的大蛇」，不時升至大地邊緣之上，仰首飲天。大蟒「埃雷」為其聖使。又一說他是尚戈的僕役，專司把地上之水運上雲中雷宮。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; rainbow-serpent parallel (cf. Australian Rainbow Serpent) noted by comparativists; tagged to the world-serpent motif cluster as an interpretive act. Cross-refs: norse-world-serpent-midgard.

passages.text: Oshumare is the Rainbow-god, the Great Snake of the Underneath, who comes up at times above the edge of the earth to drink water from the sky. A variety of the python, called by the Yorubas ere, is the messenger of the rainbow-god, and is sacred to him. According to some natives, Oshumare, the Rainbow, is the servant of Shango, his office being to take up water from the earth to the palace in the clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oke and the Self-Sealing Cavern of Abeokuta
title.zh: 奧凱與阿貝奧庫塔的自閉石洞

region.en: Abeokuta, Nigeria (the rocky cavern of the mountain god)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿貝奧庫塔（山神岩洞）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: Oke, the god of mountains, rolls down boulders and sweeps landslips on the forgetful; a falling rock is always his handiwork and a sign that something is required. At Abeokuta a rocky cavern is his shrine, and the other tribes believe that when the Egbas are defeated in war they can retire into it, which then hermetically seals itself until the danger is past.
summary.zh: 山神奧凱若遭怠慢，便滾石砸屋、土崩掩舍；落石從來都是他的手筆，也是「該有所奉獻」的警示。阿貝奧庫塔有一處岩洞即其聖所；別族相傳，埃格巴人戰敗時可退入洞中，洞門自合，封閉至險情過去。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Abeokuta (founded 1830 as a war refuge) literally means under-the-rock; the cavern legend explains the city's own name.

passages.text: Oke, mountain, or hill, is the god of Mountains, and is worshipped by those who live in mountainous or rocky country. If neglected, he is apt to roll down huge masses of rock upon the habitations of those who have been forgetful of his wants, or to sweep them away by a landslip. When any great mishap of this nature occurs, a human victim is offered up to turn away his anger. The falling of boulders or detached pieces of rock is always considered the handiwork of Oke and a sign that something is required. The emblem of Oke is a stone or fragment of rock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Abeokuta there is a rocky cavern in which Oke is worshipped. It is popularly believed by the other tribes that the Egbas, when defeated in war, can retire into this cavern, which then hermetically seals itself till the danger is past.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun Drives Out His Sons; Yemaja Makes Them Fish
title.zh: 日逐諸子，耶莫雅化之為魚

region.en: Yoruba sky-country (symbolic pin: where sky meets sea, off the Lagos coast)
region.zh: 約魯巴天空之境（象徵定位：拉哥斯海外天海相接處）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. III

summary.en: The stars are the daughters of the sun and moon. The boy-suns, growing up, tried to follow their father across the sky to the place where sea and sky meet — where, say the Yorubas, the white men go and fill their ships — but the Sun, jealous of his power, turned on them and tried to kill them. Some fled to Olosa, some to Olokun, and the rest to their grandmother Yemaja, who turned them into fish; so all the sons were driven out of the sky, while the daughters remain with their mother by night.
summary.zh: 星辰是日月的女兒。長大的小太陽們想跟隨父親橫越天穹，往天海相接之處——約魯巴人說，白人就是在那裡把船裝滿的——但太陽怕大權旁落，回頭便要殺他們。有的逃到奧洛薩處，有的投奔奧洛貢，其餘的躲進祖母耶莫雅懷裡，被她化作游魚。諸子盡逐於天外，女兒們則夜夜伴著母親。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; celestial-family myth recorded 1894. Tagged sun-capture as nearest cluster motif (jealous sun expelling rival suns).

passages.text: According to the myth, the sun, moon, and stars came from the body of Yemaja. Orun, the Sun, and Oshu, the Moon, are gods. The stars are the daughters of the sun and moon. The boys, or young suns, on growing up tried to follow their father in his course across the sky to where the sea and the sky meet, and which, say the Yorubas, is the place where the white men go and find all the things with which they fill their ships; but he, jealous of his power, turned upon them and tried to kill them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of them sought refuge with Olosa, some with Olokun, and the remainder with their grandmother, Yemaja, who turned them into fish. Thus all the sons were driven out of the sky, but the daughters remained with their mother and still accompany her by night. To see the new moon is lucky, and an eclipse of the moon is supposed to indicate that the sun is beating her, steps being taken to drive him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. III (1894); not verbatim.
